      </div>

      <h2 class="case-title">Workforce Reward &amp; Job Satisfaction Analysis</h2>

      <p class="case-question">Which reward and workplace factors are associated with job satisfaction, and how can employers use the evidence to prioritise action within budget constraints?</p>

      <div class="case-grid">
        <div class="case-block case-block-wide">
          <span class="case-block-label">Evidence</span>
          <p class="case-block-body data">21,981 WERS responses · 21,784 valid job-satisfaction records · Weighted analysis · Regression · Decision-tree sensitivity check · 22 SQL checks · 4-page Power BI dashboard · Advisory report</p>
        </div>
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Stack</span>
          <p class="case-block-body data">R · SQL · Power BI · Excel</p>
          <a href="https://github.com/catherine-echendu/workforce-reward-satisfaction-analysis" class="btn btn-primary btn-sm case-cta" target="_blank" rel="noopener">View on GitHub</a>
          <a href="https://github.com/catherine-echendu/workforce-reward-satisfaction-analysis/blob/main/05_powerbi/wers_reward_satisfaction_dashboard.pdf" class="btn btn-ghost btn-sm case-cta" target="_blank" rel="noopener">View dashboard PDF</a>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="case-grid">
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Outcome measure</span>
          <p class="case-block-body">I built a seven-item job-satisfaction index on a 1–5 scale, where 5 indicates the highest satisfaction. The final weighted mean was <span class="data">3.65/5</span> (95% CI 3.62–3.67), based on <span class="data">21,784</span> valid index records from the <span class="data">21,981</span>-employee dataset.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Training gradient</span>
          <p class="case-block-body">Weighted mean job satisfaction rose across training groups: <span class="data">3.46</span> (none), <span class="data">3.52</span> (under 1 day), <span class="data">3.66</span> (1–2 days), <span class="data">3.78</span> (3–5 days), <span class="data">3.85</span> (6–9 days), and <span class="data">4.00</span> (10+ days). Training was the only positive benefit lever in the final weighted model.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="case-grid">
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Pay evidence</span>
          <p class="case-block-body">In the adjusted model, pay satisfaction had about <span class="data">3.6×</span> the effect estimate of grouped pay band. This points to pay experience as an important line of enquiry, not simply pay level.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Segment analysis</span>
          <p class="case-block-body">The weighted decision-tree sensitivity check identified a segment representing <span class="data">5.1%</span> of the workforce with a <span class="data">61.8%</span> probability of low satisfaction: pay dissatisfaction, low training and 26+ contracted hours. This is a group-level signal for investigation, not a diagnosis of individuals.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="case-grid">
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Cross-tool validation</span>
          <p class="case-block-body"><span class="data">22/22</span> independent SQL cross-validation checks passed. The maximum observed R-versus-SQL difference across checked outputs was <span class="data">0.005</span>.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="case-block">
          <span class="case-block-label">Limitations</span>
          <p class="case-block-body">WERS is observational survey data from 2011; associations do not prove causation and should not be treated as a current workforce forecast. Flexi-time and job-sharing measures had higher missingness (10.9% and 17.5%), so those results need particular caution.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <p class="case-note">Decision relevance: the results help leaders investigate pay experience and training as potential priorities, then test those options against their own workforce, budget and operating context. The source microdata is not redistributed; the public repository contains code, documentation and aggregated outputs.</p>
    </article>
